section.title: Friendship with the World
section.sectionRationale: The wisdom from below now shows its fruit: quarrels and fights among believers. James traces conflict to warring desires, unmasks worldliness as spiritual adultery and enmity with God, and then, at the letter's turning point, sounds the gospel of grace to the humble. He issues a string of urgent calls to repent, submit, and draw near, and warns against the pride of slander and judging that usurps God's throne.
section.thesis: Fights among God's people flow from selfish cravings and friendship with the world, which is enmity against God; yet He gives more grace to the humble, so we must submit, draw near, and repent, ceasing to judge as though we were the Lawgiver.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the source of quarrels in warring desire; friendship with the world and the greater grace God gives; and the call to humble repentance and to stop judging one another.

verses.text: What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the {{hedone|passions}} at war within you?
You crave what you do not have; you kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You quarrel and fight. You do not have, because you do not ask.
And when you do ask, you do not receive, because you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures.

units.label: Friendship with the world
units.note: enmity with God, yet more grace

verses.text: You adulteresses! Do you not know that {{philia|friendship}} with the world is hostility toward God? Therefore, whoever chooses to be a friend of the world renders himself an enemy of God.
Or do you think the Scripture says without reason that the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns with envy?
But He gives us more {{charis|grace}}. This is why it says: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Grieve, mourn, and weep. Turn your laughter to mourning, and your joy to gloom.
{{tapeinos|Humble}} yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you.

Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it.
There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?

hedone.gloss: Pleasure, desire, the craving for gratification; the root of the word hedonism. James says fights among believers come from these passions warring within, and that even prayers fail when aimed at squandering God's gifts on such pleasures. Disordered desire is the hidden engine of conflict.

philia.gloss: Friendship, affectionate love, close alliance. Friendship with the world means adopting its values and loves in opposition to God, and James calls it spiritual adultery and enmity with God. One cannot be the intimate friend of the world and the friend of God at once.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's unmerited favor and enabling help. At the letter's turning point James declares that God gives more grace, greater than the pull of sin, to those who humble themselves. Grace is God's answer to the proud, self-seeking heart: He resists the proud but pours favor on the lowly.

tapeinos.gloss: Humble, lowly, of low position. God gives grace to the tapeinos and exalts those who humble themselves before Him. Humility is the posture that receives grace, the opposite of the pride God opposes; it is the doorway back from friendship with the world to fellowship with God.

basic.context: James asks where all the fighting in the church comes from, and he answers bluntly: from your own cravings at war inside you. You want things you cannot get, so you quarrel; you do not have because you do not ask, and when you do ask, you ask selfishly. Then he lands the hardest word: to be a friend of the world, cozy with its values against God, is spiritual adultery and makes you God's enemy. But right there, at the low point, comes the best news: God gives more grace. He opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. So James pleads: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, wash your hands, humble yourself, and stop setting yourself up as judge over others.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the turning point of the letter, and it is heavily prescriptive, packed with about ten imperatives calling for repentance. The key is to read it as a summons to humility that ends in grace, not merely a scolding. The shocking word adulteresses is covenant language: God's people are His bride, so loving the world is unfaithfulness. Verse 5 is famously hard to translate, but the flow is clear, God is a jealous lover of His people, and He gives greater grace.
basic.originalLanguages: The conflicts spring from hedone, pleasures or cravings, warring within. The root sin is philia, friendship, with the world, which is enmity toward God. Against the proud God sets charis, grace, more grace, given to the tapeinos, the humble. The passage moves from disordered desire to worldliness to the grace that meets the lowly.
basic.typology: The image of God's people as an unfaithful wife recalls the prophets, especially Hosea, and points to Christ the faithful Bridegroom who wins back an adulterous bride. Drawing near to God fulfills the longing of the old covenant worshiper and is opened fully through Christ. The exaltation of the humble anticipates the pattern of Christ, who humbled Himself and was exalted.
basic.christ: Grace to the humble is grace that comes through Christ, who Himself took the lowest place and was exalted, and who calls the weary to Himself. The faithful Bridegroom who reclaims an adulterous people is the Lord Jesus, who loved the church and gave Himself for her. Through Him alone can enemies of God draw near and be received.
basic.god: God is revealed as a jealous lover of His people, grieved by their friendship with the world, yet lavish in grace to the humble. He resists the proud and lifts up the lowly. He is the one Lawgiver and Judge, able to save and to destroy, so that human judging of others is a proud theft of His throne. Draw near to Him, James promises, and He will draw near to you.
basic.crossReferences: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble is quoted from Proverbs 3:34 and repeated in 1 Peter 5:5-6. Jesus said no one can serve two masters, God and the world, Matthew 6:24. James 4:10 echoes 1 Peter 5:6. And do not judge, lest you be judged, comes from Matthew 7:1.
basic.oneStory: God has always sought a faithful people and grieved over their flirtation with idols and the world, from Israel's spiritual adultery to the church's worldliness. James stands in that prophetic line but points to the gospel remedy: God gives more grace to the humble. The way home from being God's enemy is repentance and lowliness, opened by Christ the faithful Bridegroom, who humbled Himself, was exalted, and draws near to all who draw near to God.

context.literary:
James 4:1 to 12 is the most densely commanded paragraph in the letter, and its structure repays slow reading. It begins with two questions (verse 1), answers them with accusations (verses 2 to 4), pauses on a hard scriptural appeal (verse 5), and then turns on the word 'but' in verse 6 into a run of ten imperatives in verses 7 to 10, followed by a closing prohibition with two questions in verses 11 and 12. The turning point is the sentence 'But He gives us more grace.' Everything before it is diagnosis, everything after it is response, and the grace of verse 6 stands between them as the reason the response is possible.

The ten commands are almost all aorist imperatives, urgent and decisive, and they are arranged in matching pairs. Submit and resist (verse 7). Draw near, with the promise that God will draw near (verse 8a). Cleanse hands and purify hearts (verse 8b), which pairs outward conduct with inward motive. Grieve, mourn and weep, then turn laughter to mourning (verse 9). Humble yourselves (verse 10). The paragraph ends where it begins, with the same word. The command to humble yourselves in verse 10 answers the quotation about the proud and humble in verse 6, and together they enclose the whole call to repentance like brackets.

The first half also has a pattern. 'Do not have' and 'do not receive' in verses 2 and 3 are matched by the double 'because', so James produces a tight logic of failed asking: you lack because you do not ask, and you do not receive because you ask for the wrong reason. The accusation of verse 4, the single address 'adulteresses', is the sharpest word in the letter and is meant to break a cycle of self justifying complaint.

Finally, the passage grows directly out of 3:13 to 18. There wisdom from below produced disorder, and here the disorder is named: conflicts, quarrels, fights. The 'passions' of verse 1 are the 'jealousy and selfish ambition' of 3:14 under another name. Chapter 4 is not a new topic, and the rotting of the church in 4:1 is the harvest of the wrong seed in 3:16.
context.historical:
The people addressed are Jewish believers living outside Palestine, in small gatherings that met in homes and synagogues. Their social position was fragile: poor, dependent on the goodwill of employers and landlords, and sometimes dragged before magistrates, James 2:6. In societies built on honour, status disputes were common, and a group with little to fight over often fights over reputation. The fights James describes are probably verbal and relational. Some interpreters take 'you kill' as literal violence, and some see in the Jewish world of the time a climate in which factions that used force were not far off. Others take it as a startling way to say that hatred and murder are one root, as Jesus said in Matthew 5:21 and 22, and as John says of hate in 1 John 3:15. Either reading fits James's habit of speaking in ethical absolutes.

The image of adultery would have landed with force. A Jewish audience knew that the prophets repeatedly called Israel the unfaithful wife of the Lord. Hosea was told to love a woman who was unfaithful as an acted sign, Hosea 3:1, which the BSB footnote on verse 4 points to. Jeremiah said 'as a woman may betray her husband, so you have betrayed Me, O house of Israel', Jeremiah 3:20, Ezekiel 16:32 said 'You adulterous wife! You receive strangers instead of your own husband!', and Isaiah 54:5 said 'your husband is your Maker'. For readers raised on those texts, friendship with the world was not a minor failing. It was the old sin of Israel, and they would have recognised the voice.

'The world' here is not the physical creation or the whole human race. It is the world as an order of values organised without God, the same sense found in 1 John 2:15 to 17 and Galatians 1:4, the 'present evil age'. For diaspora Jews the pressure to adopt the values of the surrounding culture was constant, whether in business, in honour, or in the security of power.

The calls to grieve and mourn belong to the ritual vocabulary of repentance in Israel, where fasting and sackcloth accompanied a return to the Lord, as in Joel 2:12 and 13. James wants a response that costs something visible, in contrast to casual religiosity.
context.canonical:
The paragraph is thick with Scripture, some of it quoted and some of it echoed. Verse 6 quotes Proverbs 3:34, a text James and Peter both lean on: 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble', 1 Peter 5:5 and 6. The BSB footnote notes that James follows the wording of the Greek Old Testament, which has 'the proud' where the Hebrew has 'mockers'. Both set a proud heart against the God who gives grace.

The language of drawing near and returning belongs to the prophets. 'Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you', Zechariah 1:3, and the same in Malachi 3:7. James's promise that God will draw near to those who draw near is that covenant promise compressed. The verses on clean hands and pure hearts echo Psalm 24:3 and 4, where the one who may ascend the hill of the LORD has 'clean hands and a pure heart', and Isaiah 1:16, 'Wash and cleanse yourselves.' James also uses the word for double minded that he used in 1:8, tying repentance back to the opening call to ask in faith.

The 'one Lawgiver and Judge' of verse 12 resonates with Isaiah 33:22, 'the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us.' James brings Judge, lawgiver and saviour together in the same sentence, as Isaiah did. Paul makes a related argument when he asks, 'Who are you to judge someone else's servant?', Romans 14:4.

Jesus taught the same pattern in His own words: 'whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted', Luke 14:11 and Matthew 23:12. James's 'He will exalt you' in verse 10 is a clear echo, and Peter's 'Humble yourselves, therefore, under God's mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you', 1 Peter 5:6, is the same teaching at its best. James's command to resist the devil also has a counterpart in Peter, 1 Peter 5:9, and Paul's call to stand against the devil's schemes, Ephesians 6:11.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
James wants to break a habit of blaming outwards. Believers who fight usually have an account of why it is someone else's fault, and verse 1 refuses the account by asking where the fight comes from, then answering that the fighting begins within each person. The thing he wants his readers to see is that behind the argument about who said what is a desire that has gone unchecked, and that the church's wars are only private wars made public.

He also intends to expose a divided loyalty. Prayer in verses 2 and 3 is treated as a test: the motive behind the request shows whom the person actually serves. Someone asking God for what he wants to burn on his pleasures is trying to use God as an instrument of the world's agenda. James calls that adultery because it is not mere weakness but a transfer of allegiance.

The deepest intention is pastoral and hopeful. A letter that only condemned would produce despair, so James places 'more grace' in the middle, and every command after it is a response to that grace. The person who is told to submit, draw near and humble himself is being invited back by a God who is already at the door. The simple promise 'He will draw near to you' tells the reader why the repentance is worth it.

Finally, James brings the argument back to speech. By ending with the ban on slander and judging, he shows that the pride described earlier is practised daily in how believers talk about each other. He wants his readers to see that a person who tears down a brother has quietly assumed a seat that is not his.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is overwhelmingly prescriptive, and the commands are for every believer, but the application needs thought about whom they address. They are addressed to people who have grown comfortable in a worldly manner of living and need to be shaken awake, not to the struggling person who is already grieving his sin. Taken out of context, 'Grieve, mourn, and weep' can crush a tender conscience. In context it is a call to stop treating sin lightly, and the verse that follows promises exaltation.

Not every desire is condemned. James does not forbid asking God for things, or wanting things, since verse 2 says the lack comes partly from not asking. The problem is the motive, 'that you may squander it on your pleasures'. Application therefore means examining why we pray as we do, not giving up prayer for comfort or provision. The prohibition on judging in verse 11 is also narrower than it looks. James is not banning discernment or moral conviction, and he himself judges plainly in this very paragraph. The ban is on slander and on setting oneself up as the lawgiver.

Finally, the passage describes the pattern of grace, not a ladder to earn it. God's grace in verse 6 comes before the commands, so they are not the price of grace but its fruit. Believers today apply the passage whenever they feel the pull of the culture's measure of success, and whenever they notice themselves running the same case against a brother in their own head.

debates.question: What does the difficult verse 5 mean about the Spirit yearning with envy?

views.label: God jealously yearns over the spirit He put in us
views.case: Many read it of God's own jealous love: the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns jealously for our undivided devotion, which fits the charge of adultery and the promise of greater grace. God is a jealous lover who will not share His bride with the world.

views.label: The human spirit tends toward envy
views.case: Others take it of the human spirit's bent to envious craving, describing the sinful pull that friendship with the world feeds. Either reading leads into verse 6: but He gives more grace.

debates.bearing: The verse is genuinely hard, but the argument is clear either way. Whether it speaks of God's jealousy for us or our bent to envy, the answer is the greater grace God gives to the humble.

debates.question: Does forbidding judging in verses 11 to 12 rule out all discernment?

views.label: No; it forbids proud, condemning judgment
views.case: James condemns slander and setting oneself up as judge over a brother, usurping the place of the one Lawgiver and Judge. It does not forbid the discernment and loving correction the letter itself calls for, but the self-exalting judgment that plays God.

views.label: It targets judging that dismisses God's law
views.case: Others stress the specific logic: to condemn a brother is to act as judge over the law itself, as if one stood above it. The sin is arrogating an authority that belongs to God alone.

debates.bearing: Both agree the ban is on proud, God-usurping condemnation, not on wise discernment or the restoration of a wanderer that James commends in chapter 5.

study.originalLanguages:
The first verse uses the vocabulary of war twice. 'Conflicts' and 'quarrels' translate polemoi and machai, and the verb behind 'at war within you' is strateuomai, to serve as a soldier on campaign. Peter uses it of the desires of the flesh which 'war against your soul', 1 Peter 2:11. The BSB footnote reads verse 1 'literally passions warring among your members', and 'members' can mean the limbs of the body or the members of the congregation. James may be deliberately letting both senses stand: the war in the body is the war in the church.

In verse 2 the verbs come in pairs and escalate. 'Crave' is epithumeo, the desire of the tenth commandment. 'Kill' is phoneuo, and 'covet' translates zeloo, the verb from the same family as zelos, jealousy, in 3:14. So the 'jealousy' of the last chapter is here shown in action. The climb runs from craving to killing, and the verb zeloo shows that envy is the engine.

Verse 4 uses the feminine moichalides, 'adulteresses'. Many later manuscripts add 'adulterers and', which may be a scribe's effort to include everyone. The feminine form carries the covenant picture of Israel as the bride. The word 'world' is kosmos, which in James 1:27 and 3:6 and here means the ordered system of human life apart from God. Reading 4:4 with 1 John 2:15, 'If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him', shows the word is shared across the New Testament.

Verse 5 is the notorious puzzle. It begins 'Or do you think the Scripture says without reason', but no Old Testament verse reads like the sentence that follows. The next clause 'the Spirit He caused to dwell in us yearns with envy' turns on two decisions. First, the verb 'caused to dwell' is transitive in the reading the BSB follows, and the footnote 'Or the spirit' admits that 'spirit' may be human or divine. Second, 'envy' is phthonos, which is almost always a vice, and the verb 'yearns' (epipotheo) is usually positive, used for longing in 2 Corinthians 9:14 and elsewhere. It is therefore reasonable to ask whether God is the one who yearns, with a zealous jealousy of the kind the Law attributes to Him: 'I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God', Exodus 20:5, and Deuteronomy 6:15 and 32:16 to 21 where His people provoke it by turning to other gods.

Verse 6 turns on the verb antitassetai, 'opposes', a military term meaning to line up in battle order against. In verse 7 the believer resists the devil with a different verb, antistete, and in verse 6 God opposes the proud with antitassetai. So the proud, who think they are standing against God's way, find God drawn up against them. In verse 7 'submit' is hypotasso, the opposite of a military array, to place oneself under authority in an ordered rank.

In verse 8 'double-minded' is dipsychos, literally two souled, a word found in the New Testament only in James, here and in 1:8. 'Purify' is hagnizo, from the same root as the 'pure' of 3:17.

Verse 11 'slander' is katalaleo, to speak against, and 'judge' is krino. James then puts two nouns side by side, poietes and krites, a doer of the law and a judge of it. The word poietes recalls the 'doers of the word' in 1:22 to 25. To judge your brother, James says, is to stop being a doer and become a critic, and to take the place of the one 'Lawgiver and Judge', nomothetes and krites, the pair that Isaiah 33:22 gave to the LORD.

typology.fulfillment: The prophets painted the covenant as a marriage and Israel's idolatry as adultery, Jeremiah 3:20, Ezekiel 16:32 and Hosea 3:1. James turns the picture on believers who befriend the world. The correspondence reaches its fulfilment in Christ the faithful Bridegroom, who 'loved the church and gave Himself up for her to make her holy', Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and for whom the church is presented 'as a pure virgin', 2 Corinthians 11:2. The type is incomplete because Israel's marriage failed again and again, while the new covenant is kept by the Bridegroom's own fidelity, so the bride is secure because she is held, not because she is perfect.

typology.type: The priests who draw near with clean hands
typology.fulfillment: In the Old Testament only those prepared by washing and purification could approach the Lord, and Psalm 24:3 and 4 asks who may ascend His hill. James takes the pattern to every believer, calling for washed hands and a purified heart before drawing near. It is fulfilled in Christ our high priest, so that 'we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus', Hebrews 10:19 to 22, with 'hearts sprinkled clean'. The old pattern cleansed the body; the new cleanses the conscience. It falls short as a type because the priests came on behalf of others and returned to a distant God, whereas believers draw near through a priest who ever lives to intercede.

Israel's repentance often moved through fasting and mourning toward restoration, as in Joel 2:12 to 14 and Nehemiah 9, and verse 10 ties humbling to exaltation. The pattern is perfected in Christ, who 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death', and then 'God exalted Him to the highest place', Philippians 2:8 and 9. He is the one in whom the 'He will exalt you' of verse 10 is first kept, and those who are united to Him share in it, Romans 8:17. The type falls short in that the first humbling in Israel was for sin, while Christ's was for the sins of others.

Pharaoh, Babylon and the rulers who set themselves against the Lord's anointed display the shape of verse 6, where those who exalt themselves are brought down. Mary's song gathers the pattern: 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble', Luke 1:52. It is fulfilled finally at the cross, where the powers that thought they had won were disarmed, Colossians 2:15, and the humbled Servant was lifted up. The correspondence falls short of a final form until the last day, when 'every knee should bow', Philippians 2:10, and all pride is ended.

study.christ:
The paragraph leads to Christ first as the answer to the question of verse 5 and verse 6, where the grace that comes to the humble has a name. 'He gives us more grace' is the gospel in four words. Where does the extra grace come from? Paul says it is 'the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor', 2 Corinthians 8:9. Grace that outweighs the believer's friendship with the world is grace that was paid for by Someone who refused the world's offer. In the wilderness the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and offered them for a single act of worship, and Jesus said 'Away from Me, Satan!', Matthew 4:10. The one man who was truly a friend of God and no friend of the world's system is the one who made it possible for the rest of us to be reconciled.

The imperative 'Humble yourselves' is Christ's own path. Philippians 2:5 to 11 is the best commentary on verses 6 and 10: He 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death' and 'God exalted Him to the highest place'. His own teaching gives the same line: 'whoever humbles himself will be exalted', Matthew 23:12. James can say 'He will exalt you' because the Exalted One has gone ahead and carried humility to its lowest point, the cross.

Verse 7 speaks of resisting the devil so that he flees, and Christ is the pattern as well as the power. The tempter 'left Him', and angels came to minister to Him, Matthew 4:11. We resist because He resisted, and because His victory means the enemy's final flight is guaranteed.

The picture of the unfaithful wife is answered in Him. The Bridegroom who comes for an adulterous bride does not divorce her but dies for her, Ephesians 5:25 to 27, and says 'I will betroth you to Me forever', as Hosea 2:19 puts it. The same grace that calls the church an adulteress also washes her.

On the question of judging in verses 11 and 12, Christ is the Lawgiver and Judge. 'The Father judges no one, but has entrusted all judgment to the Son', John 5:22. He alone is 'able to save and destroy', and He is the One who saved, so even the right to condemn is exercised through mercy: 'God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him', John 3:17. The only person with a right to judge is also the only one who took the sentence upon himself.

A caution: not every phrase in the paragraph is about Jesus. The point of verses 7 to 10 is repentance, and it should not be allegorised into scenes from the Gospels. But the God who draws near to the one who draws near is the God who drew near most fully when the Word became flesh.
study.god:
This paragraph shows a God of covenant love who is jealous because He is committed. The jealousy of verse 5, on either reading, is not petty. In the Law it is the jealousy of a husband whose wife has gone after others, Exodus 20:5 and Deuteronomy 6:15, and it is bound up with His grace. A God without jealousy would be a God who did not care whether His people were His. That the Lord of heaven wants us is both the cause of the warning and the reason for the promise.

It shows a God who opposes the proud. The verb is a military one, and James is not describing a mild disapproval. The cold edge of that verb is part of the doctrine of God: He resists every claim to His throne. It shows at once that He 'gives grace to the humble'. The two halves belong to one character. His grace does not coexist with pride, and His opposition to pride is the necessary shadow of His giving, since a heart that is full of itself has no room to receive.

It shows a God who is accessible. 'Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you' is the promise Zechariah and Malachi spoke for the Lord of Hosts, and it carries a staggering assumption, that the Almighty answers the first small step. Psalm 34:18 says 'The LORD is near to the brokenhearted', and Isaiah 57:15 gives the same truth from the throne: the high and holy One dwells 'with the oppressed and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly'. The very God who resists the proud is the God who lives with the lowly.

It shows a God who is the one lawgiver and judge. James's argument in verses 11 and 12 is theological: the right to condemn belongs to the one who is able both to save and to destroy, and no brother has that power. This is a statement of God's sovereignty, but also of His fitness. Only a Judge who can save can be trusted to judge. That keeps judgment from being arbitrary and mercy from being weak.

It shows a God who hears prayer, since the problem in verse 3 is wrong motives and not a lack of listening. He is not deaf, but He is not a servant, and He does not hand over what would harm the asker. In the doctrine of prayer this paragraph puts God's wisdom above the petitioner's wish.

For worship this means that repentance is itself praise. To humble oneself under the mighty hand, 1 Peter 5:6, is to say that He is God and we are not. And because He gives more grace, worship in this key is never gloomy: the mourning of verse 9 is the doorway to the exaltation of verse 10, and the person who has been humbled is the one who sings.

crossReferences.note: The jealousy and selfish ambition of the previous paragraph, with its disorder and every vile practice. Chapter 4:1 names the same thing, passions at war, and shows its public fruit: quarrels and fights. The two paragraphs are one argument, and each explains the other.

Peter urges exiles to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which war against the soul. It uses the same military verb as James 4:1 and supports the reading that the battleground is first inside each believer, with the church's conflicts as the visible spillover.

The BSB footnote on verse 4 points here. The Lord tells the prophet to love a woman loved by another and an adulteress, in the way the LORD loves the Israelites, though they turn to other gods. It shows that the charge of adultery is made by a God who has not stopped loving the one He charges.

I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God. This is the base text for verse 5 on the reading that God yearns. His jealousy is a covenant jealousy, the zeal of a faithful husband who will not share His people, and it is the opposite of the envy that makes human fights.

The verse James quotes in verse 6. The Hebrew says He mocks the mockers and gives grace to the humble, and James, following the Greek, says God opposes the proud. It shows that his claim 'more grace' is not new teaching but the settled character of God from Israel's wisdom.

Peter quotes the same Proverbs text and runs the same sequence as James: humble yourselves under God's mighty hand, and resist the devil, standing firm. The parallel suggests a shared body of teaching in the early church and shows the commands work together.

Return to Me, says the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you. James's promise that God will draw near to those who draw near is this covenant invitation. Malachi 3:7 repeats it, so the text is a standing offer to a people who feel far away.

Who may ascend the hill of the LORD? The one with clean hands and a pure heart. James asks for both together, and by calling the double minded to purify the heart he shows that outward cleansing is not enough without inward single mindedness.

The LORD is our Judge, our lawgiver, our King, and He will save us. James 4:12 uses the same trio of roles for the one Lawgiver and Judge who is able to save, and so places his warning against human judging within Isaiah's confession of God's rule.

Who are you to judge someone else's servant? To his own master he stands or falls. Paul makes the argument James makes in verse 12, that the believer is another's servant, and adds the comfort that the Lord is able to make him stand.

Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. It is the saying behind verses 6 and 10, and it shows James has taken a principle straight from Jesus' own teaching and set it at the climax of his call to repentance.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with one friendship. In Genesis 2 the man and woman walked with God without shame, and Genesis 3 shows what friendship with another voice does. The serpent offered wisdom and independence, the pair listened, and the first result was hiding, then blame, then a murder in the next generation. James 4:1 to 4 is the same sequence at the scale of a congregation: desire, rivalry, violence, and a broken relationship with the God who made them.

God's response across the Old Testament is to marry His people. At Sinai He binds Himself to Israel, and the prophets use the language of husband and wife to describe the covenant. Then they describe the betrayal: Israel chases other lovers, and the Lord woos her back. Hosea buys back his wife, Jeremiah and Ezekiel indict, and Isaiah says the Maker is the husband. The line of promise through all of it is that the God who is jealous is also the God who will betroth His people 'in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion', Hosea 2:19.

The New Testament keeps the same drama and gives it its climax. Christ comes as the Bridegroom, takes the penalty of the adulterous bride, and washes her. James is writing to a church that has been redeemed and is still tempted back to its old loves. He therefore calls for the repentance that belongs to the covenant, and promises that the God of the covenant is near.

Humility is the way through the whole story. The first Adam grasped at being like God; the last Adam 'did not consider equality with God something to be grasped', and God exalted Him, Philippians 2:6 to 9. The church lives between the humbling and the exaltation, resisting the devil, drawing near, and refusing to take the judge's seat.

The story ends with a wedding. Revelation pictures the bride made ready and the Lamb's marriage, Revelation 19:7 and 21:2, a world where the friendship with God is unbroken and the world's counterfeit has been judged. Then the proud have no throne, the humble inherit the earth, and God Himself is the Judge and the Lawgiver whose verdicts nobody questions. Until then, the grace of verse 6 is on offer, and it is always more than the sin.

quiz.q: Where does James say the quarrels among believers come from?

options.text: From their own passions and cravings at war within them.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2: conflict springs from disordered desire inside us.

options.text: From wanting things they cannot get, so they fight to obtain them.
options.note: True to verse 2, describing how the craving works out.

options.text: From other people who provoke them unfairly.
options.note: James locates the root within, not merely in others.

options.text: From God withholding good things arbitrarily.
options.note: They lack because they do not ask, or ask wrongly, not because God is stingy.

quiz.q: Why does James call friendship with the world so serious?

options.text: Because it is spiritual adultery and makes one an enemy of God.
options.note: Verse 4: loving the world is enmity toward God.

options.text: Because one cannot be a friend of the world and of God at once.
options.note: True to the logic, echoing serving two masters.

options.text: Because the world has nothing good in it whatsoever.
options.note: The issue is divided love and allegiance, not that creation is evil.

options.text: Because God does not really mind where our loyalties lie.
options.note: The opposite: God is a jealous lover of His people.

quiz.q: What is the turning-point good news in verse 6?

options.text: God gives more grace; He opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
options.note: Verse 6: greater grace for the lowly is the hinge of the passage.

options.text: God's grace is greater than the pull of our sin.
options.note: True to the promise, though it omits the proud-humble contrast.

options.text: God gives grace only to those who first prove themselves.
options.note: Grace goes to the humble, not the self-proven.

options.text: God leaves the proud and humble to the same fate.
options.note: He opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble, a real difference.

quiz.q: What does James command in verses 7 to 10?

options.text: Submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, and humble yourselves in repentance.
options.note: Verses 7 to 10: a cascade of calls to humble repentance.

options.text: Draw near to God with the promise that He will draw near to you.
options.note: True from verse 8, one part of the fuller call.

options.text: Wait passively for God to change you without any response.
options.note: The passage is full of active imperatives to repent and turn.

options.text: Assert yourself so that God will be forced to bless you.
options.note: The call is to humble yourself, and He will exalt you.

quiz.q: Why does James forbid judging one another in verses 11 to 12?

options.text: Because there is one Lawgiver and Judge, and to condemn a brother usurps God's place.
options.note: Verse 12: judging others steals the authority of the one Judge.

options.text: Because speaking against a brother sets oneself above the law itself.
options.note: True to verse 11, another angle on the same pride.

options.text: Because Christians should never discern right from wrong at all.
options.note: James forbids proud condemnation, not wise discernment.

options.text: Because no one ever does anything worth correcting.
options.note: The issue is who has the right to judge, not that sin is unreal.

questions: James traces fights to cravings at war within us. Behind a recent conflict of yours, what desire were you really fighting to protect or obtain?
Friendship with the world is subtle. Where have you grown comfortable with values or loves that quietly compete with your devotion to God?
God gives more grace to the humble. What would it look like this week to come to Him low and empty rather than proud and self-sufficient?
The passage calls us to draw near to God with the promise that He will draw near to us. What is one concrete way you could draw near this week?
Where are you tempted to sit as judge over a brother or sister? How does remembering the one Lawgiver and Judge change how you speak about them?

translationNotes.note: Passions renders hedone, pleasures or cravings; a footnote gives the literal passions warring among your members, picturing an internal war that erupts in outward conflict.
Adulteresses draws on the prophetic image of God's people as an unfaithful wife; a footnote points to Hosea 3:1. It frames worldliness as covenant unfaithfulness.

This verse is notoriously difficult; it may speak of God's jealous yearning over the spirit He placed in us, or of the human spirit's bent to envy. The following verse resolves it: but He gives more grace.
The quotation, God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, is from Proverbs 3:34, printed as poetry in the BSB and set here as running prose.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for James 4:1-12. The poetic couplet in verse 6 is set as running prose.
